events.title: The Fed raises interest rates
events.description: Its target for short-term interest rates rises from 1% to 1.25% as the economy grows and job conditions improve.

events.title: Microsoft plans payments to shareholders
events.description: The company announces regular dividends, a one-time $3 payment per share and plans to buy back some of its shares.

events.title: Apple introduces the iPhone
events.description: A new touchscreen device combines a phone, music player and internet functions.

events.title: Economists announce a recession
events.description: Researchers say the economy stopped expanding in December 2007. Their announcement comes a year later.

events.title: The Fed cuts rates close to zero
events.description: The Federal Reserve lowers its short-term target to 0–0.25% as the economy and lending conditions worsen.

what_happened_next.text:
The five years after May 2004 brought economic growth, higher interest rates and then a serious financial crisis. A recession had begun in December 2007, but the official announcement came a year later. The window ends in May 2009, while families and businesses were still facing a difficult period.

The companies changed in different ways. Apple reported one million iPhones sold in the first 74 days after launch. Microsoft reported $51.12 billion in fiscal-2007 revenue, up 15%, with customer acceptance of Vista and Office among the reasons. eBay recorded a roughly $1.4 billion charge tied to Skype after buying the service in 2005. Product sales and accounting losses are useful clues, but they do not explain every move in a share price.

The investment results were far apart: one dollar in Apple ended near $9.68, Microsoft near 96 cents and eBay near 40 cents. A popular product or familiar company did not guarantee a winning investment. No one at the May 2004 start knew exactly how the economy, software, phones or internet calling would change over the next five years.

reflection.what_people_were_focused_on: The May headlines covered jobs, expensive gas, Iraq, the coming election, cicadas, movies, and sports. Investors were also watching companies such as Apple, Microsoft, and eBay.
reflection.what_actually_mattered: The economy went from steady growth to a deep crisis. The companies also made different choices and faced different challenges. What people expected in 2004 could not tell them exactly how each investment would turn out.
reflection.what_faded_away: Election and sports days came and went, and the cicadas appeared for a short time. The financial trouble that came later lasted longer and changed the economy. A busy news story could not tell anyone which investment would do best.
reflection.what_nobody_knew: In May 2004, no one knew when the financial crisis would arrive, how low interest rates would go, whether people would take to the iPhone, or how each company would do. The recession had already begun before its official start date was announced.

hot:2004-05:apple.text: Apple said on September 10, 2007, that it had sold its millionth iPhone in the first 74 days after launch. Its touch-screen phone joined calling and internet features with Apple’s music and computer software, giving the company a new product business with fast early sales.

hot:2004-05:microsoft.text: Microsoft reported fiscal 2007 revenue of $51.12 billion, up 15%, and said sales of Windows Vista and Office 2007 helped drive growth. Customers were still buying Microsoft’s core software products as the company moved to newer versions.

hot:2004-05:ebay.text: In October 2007, eBay said quarterly results would include a roughly $1.4 billion charge on Skype, which it had bought in 2005. eBay judged Skype’s value to be lower than the amount it had recorded, showing that expected benefits from the purchase had not arrived as planned.
